summary: Explains the three client/server email models, offline, online and disconnected, and how IMAP4 can be used with each. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Three ways to use a mailbox: take mail home, read it at the post office, or take a copy home and sync later.

questions: offline vs online vs disconnected email
what are the imap4 mail models
subtitle: Three ways of doing client/server email, offline, online and disconnected, and how IMAP4 can serve all of them.

tldr.problem: Email clients and servers can divide the work and the mailbox data in very different ways, and a protocol needs to say which of those ways it supports.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the offline, online and disconnected models, compares their strengths in a table, and explains that IMAP4 transmits data on demand and relies on configuration, not protocol changes, to fit each model.
tldr.outcome: IMAP4 started out for the online model but can support all three, so one client can switch between them.

today: RFC 1733 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the models as they were understood in December 1994.

sections.title: Three Models of Email
sections.content:
There are three fundamental models of client/server email: offline, online and disconnected use. IMAP4 can be used in any of them.

The memo is informational and, like its companions, says nothing about security: its Security Considerations section states that security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: There are three basic ways to handle email between your computer and a mail server, and IMAP4 is flexible enough for each.

sections.title: Offline, Online and Disconnected
sections.content:
In the offline model, a client connects now and then, downloads all pending messages, deletes them from the server and processes everything locally. This is the familiar model used by POP-3 (RFC 1225) and UUCP, and it is store-and-forward from a maildrop to a single destination machine.

In the online model, common with remote file systems such as NFS, the client works on mailbox data on the server and keeps a connection open. No mailbox data lives on the client. IMAP4 offers a form of this that needs far less bandwidth than a remote file system and can use the server for CPU or I/O heavy work like parsing and searching.

The disconnected model, used by PCMAIL (RFC 1056), is a hybrid. The user downloads some messages, works on them offline and uploads changes later, while the server stays the authoritative store. Synchronization, especially with several clients, relies on unique identifiers for each message.
sections.eli5: Offline is taking all your letters home. Online is reading them at the post office. Disconnected is taking copies home and telling the post office what you changed later.

sections.title: Data on Demand
sections.content:
IMAP4 transmits message data only when asked and gives a client the facilities to decide what it needs. There is generally no need to move a whole mailbox or the full text of a message, which matters for large mailboxes or slow links. Because IMAP4 supports server-based RFC 822 and MIME processing, a client can learn in advance what a message contains. The memo's example is a dialup user who sees a 2000 byte text segment and a 40 megabyte video segment and fetches only the text.

The client/server relationship lasts only as long as the TCP connection, and there is no client registration. Apart from any unique identifiers used for disconnected operation, the client starts with no knowledge of mailbox state and learns it when it selects a mailbox. That first transfer is minimal.
sections.eli5: Instead of dumping the whole mailbox on you, IMAP4 shows you a list and lets you ask for just the parts you want, like fetching a short note and leaving the giant video behind.

sections.title: Where Data and State Live
sections.content:
The model chosen decides where mailbox data lives, and it also decides where message state lives, such as whether a message was read or answered. These locations need not be the same. In the online model, state can sit with the mailbox data, or it can be kept on the client or a third agent using unique identifiers as a common reference across sessions. The latter helps with a server that exports public data such as netnews and keeps no per-user state.

IMAP4 provides the generality for all this through server and especially client configuration, and does not require changes to the protocol or to its implementation.
sections.eli5: Where your mail is kept and where the "already read" marks are kept can be different places, and you can choose how to set that up.
